title: Twelve-month-olds pointed on more trials when an adult shared the sight
summary: In a lab study, 12-month-olds who already pointed did so on more trials when the adult shared attention and interest than when the adult did not.
body: Liszkowski, Carpenter, Henning, Striano, and Tomasello tested 75 German infants, average age 12 months and 6 days, whose parents had said they already pointed. Infants who never pointed in the session were not in the final count. When the adult alternated gaze and showed emotion about the event, infants pointed on a higher share of later trials than when the adult emoted only at the baby, looked only at the event, or ignored the point. Inside a single trial they repeated the point more if that sharing did not happen. The authors read this as declarative pointing, a bid to share a sight. It is one lab, and the babies were already pointers, so it is not the age when pointing first appears for most children.

sources.title: Twelve-month-olds point to share attention and interest
sources.author: Ulf Liszkowski, Malinda Carpenter, Anne Henning, Tricia Striano, and Michael Tomasello
sources.note: Supports the result that joint-attention responses drew points on more trials, and that unshared responses drew more repeats within a trial. PubMed record of the paper, opened with the abstract and results summary.
